title: Thread a spring clip collar onto a loadable dumbbell sleeve and seat it flush against the weight plate
instruction: Squeeze the spring clip collar open, thread it onto the dumbbell sleeve, slide it flush against the outer weight plate, release it so the wire jaws grip the sleeve, and clear both grippers.
context: Every home gym session uses spring clip collars to hold weight plates on a loadable dumbbell or barbell sleeve. A spring collar is a closed ring: it goes onto the sleeve only over the bar's free end, and only while both crossed wire handles are squeezed inward, because at rest its two clamp shoes are preloaded inside the sleeve. Once released the wire jaws grip the sleeve by friction, which is what stops the plates from sliding and what a bench test checks with a spring scale. Nothing about that needs a guiding aid: the collar simply has to be brought to the bar's axis from where it was set down, squared up, and pushed home while both hands keep it squeezed and the bar is held still.
setup: A 1.20 kg loadable dumbbell rests in a benchtop cradle stand: a 310 x 240 mm steel base with two polymer channel saddles 120 mm apart gripping the 28 mm knurled centre handle, so the sleeve centreline sits 80 mm above the tabletop and nothing stands in the collar's path. Both 49 mm plain round chrome loading sleeves are loaded with two rubber-coated fractional plates (134 mm and 118 mm outer diameters, 15 mm thick); the near sleeve's outer plate face is the axial stop, 26.5 mm of collar width short of the seating point. The dumbbell, the stand and the collar holster are all built along their local x and turned onto world +Y, so the right arm threads the collar straight out from its own base. A 0.320 kg three-turn chrome spring clip collar (68 mm coil centreline, two crossed spring-wire stirrup jaws, vinyl-dipped shoes and red vinyl squeeze handles 11 mm wide and 34 mm tall, 53 mm above the sleeve axis) stands upright on its coil in a felt-lined timber holster 150 mm off the sleeve axis, off the bar entirely. At rest the jaw shoes are preloaded 4 mm inside the 24.5 mm sleeve radius (2200 N/m per crossed leg), so the collar cannot be pushed onto the sleeve unsqueezed; squeezing the handles opens the shoes clear of the sleeve over a 12.5 mm stroke. One fixed starting layout; arms start at the ready pose.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial from physical end-state geometry with a feeler gauge (or ruler), and digital protractor; the run succeeds once 1.0 holds continuously for 3 s. Possible scores 0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 1.0. 1.0: the dumbbell stays seated within 12 mm horizontally and 8 mm vertically of its cradle and tilted at most 6 deg, the collar sits on the sleeve coaxial within 10 mm and 12 deg, the collar's foremost plate-side surface (its two plastic squeeze handles, the part that stands proud of the coil) is flush against the outer plate face within 3 mm, and both grippers are more than 120 mm clear of the collar and the sleeve. 0.50: the same but either the collar is more than 3 mm (up to 8 mm) off the plate face, or a gripper is still within 120 mm. 0.25: the dumbbell seated and the collar coaxial and slid at least 30 mm in along the sleeve from the free end, but not yet within 8 mm of the plate face. 0.0: otherwise (doing nothing, an unsqueezed collar stopped at the sleeve end, a collar dropped off-axis or cocked, or the dumbbell shifted out of its cradle).
reset_notes: Set the dumbbell level in the cradle with the near sleeve's outer plate face toward the robot, and stand the spring collar upright in the timber holster 150 mm off the sleeve axis, jaws at rest.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (20 Hz control). The three-turn spring collar uses a 68 mm 8-sided coil barrel with two crossed prismatic spring-wire stirrup jaws (2200 N/m per leg, 4 mm preload inside the sleeve, 12.5 mm stroke, non-overlapping handles) rather than continuous helical wire torsion; the dumbbell uses rigid primitive cylinders with a two-step end chamfer. Friction and contact softness are calibrated within 0.8x to 1.5x margin.
